50479:
Genesis says humans are made in the image and likeness of God (Gen 1:26-27), and Psalm 8 says we are crowned with glory and honour. Genesis 3 tells how that image-bearer turned from God, and the rest of Scripture shows the damage. Traditions describe the damage differently. Augustine, Luther and Calvin taught that sin affects every part of us (often called “total depravity”, which means sin touches everything, not that humans are as bad as they could be). Orthodox Christians usually say the image remains but the likeness to God is lost and must be restored. Catholics speak of a nature wounded but not destroyed. Wesleyans stress “prevenient grace”: God’s grace already at work in every person before they believe.

The New Testament adds a surprising claim: we only see the true human in Jesus. He is “the image of the invisible God” (Col 1:15), the “last Adam” (1 Cor 15:45), the one in whom we see humanity crowned with glory as Psalm 8 promised (Heb 2:6-9). Pilate said more than he knew: “Behold the man!” (John 19:5). Karl Barth built his whole doctrine of humanity on this idea: we learn what a human is from Jesus, not from Adam.

The learner’s source, Tommy Miller, puts it this way: “He is not a superhuman; he is the human.” If our anthropology starts with Adam’s failure, we will read the Bible as a manual for managing failure. If it starts with Christ, we read it as the story of God restoring his image.
50480: Tragic ontology: copying Jesus or living from him?
50481:
*Ontology* means the study of being: what something most deeply is. Tommy Miller uses the phrase “tragic ontology” for a mistake he believes is common: reading Christ’s work through Adam’s eyes. In that view, Jesus is mainly an example (his life is “exemplary”), and our task is to try harder to copy him. Miller argues that the New Testament presents Jesus’ life as “vicarious”: done on our behalf and in our place, so that we share in it. The question shifts from “What should I do?” to “Who am I in him?”

Paul’s language supports the concern. “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” (Gal 2:20). “Our old man is crucified with him” (Rom 6:6). “Ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God” (Col 3:3). “If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature” (2 Cor 5:17). These are statements of identity, not instructions. Theologians call this *union with Christ*. It is central in Calvin (who wrote that as long as Christ remains outside us, all he did is of no use to us; *Institutes* 3.1.1), in the Orthodox teaching of *theosis* (sharing in the divine nature, 2 Pet 1:4), and in the Scottish theologians T. F. and J. B. Torrance, who spoke of the “vicarious humanity of Christ”: Jesus believes, obeys and worships for us and in us.

In fairness, imitation is also biblical. Paul says, “Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor 11:1), and “be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children” (Eph 5:1). Peter says Christ left us an example (1 Pet 2:21). The issue is not whether we follow Jesus’ example but where the power comes from. The New Testament pattern is that the command flows from the identity: “you are dead and your life is hidden with Christ” (Col 3:3), therefore “put to death what is earthly” (Col 3:5). Scholars call this the *indicative* (what is true) grounding the *imperative* (what to do).
50482: John and Paul: a language of union
50483:
The learner notes that John and Paul give us a language. That is accurate. Paul’s favourite phrase is “in Christ” (with “in him” and “in the Lord” it appears well over a hundred times). John’s is “abide” or “remain”: “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4). Jesus says, “At that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you” (John 14:20). John’s first letter goes further: “as he is, so are we in this world” (1 John 4:17).

John’s Gospel also reads differently from Matthew, Mark and Luke (called the *Synoptic* Gospels, “seen together”, because they share much material and order). Around AD 200 Clement of Alexandria said that John, seeing that the outward facts had been set down, wrote a “spiritual Gospel” (recorded by Eusebius, *Church History* 6.14.7). The Gospel’s author is “the disciple whom Jesus loved”, who lay close to Jesus’ chest at the Last Supper (John 13:23-25). Church tradition from Irenaeus onward identifies him as John the son of Zebedee; many modern scholars debate this.

Two gentle corrections keep the picture balanced. The Synoptics are not mere reports: each is a carefully shaped theological portrait (Mark opens with “Jesus Christ, the Son of God”, Mark 1:1; Matthew ends with “I am with you always”, Matt 28:20). And John insists he is also a witness to real events (John 19:35; John 21:24). Still, John’s stated purpose is revelation: “that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name” (John 20:31). Both John and Paul break the idea that God stands far away from us. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor 5:19); those who were far off have been brought near (Eph 2:13).
50484: Why is there no “hell” in John or Paul?
50485:
The learner’s observation is correct. The word usually translated “hell” in the Gospels is *Gehenna*, the name of the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where children had once been sacrificed (Jer 7:31) and which became a picture of judgement. Gehenna appears twelve times in the New Testament: seven in Matthew, three in Mark, once in Luke, and once in James (Jas 3:6). It never appears in John’s Gospel or in any of Paul’s letters. Paul also never uses *Hades* (the realm of the dead) in the best manuscripts.

But John and Paul do speak of judgement, in their own words. John: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life, but whoever does not obey the Son “shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him” (John 3:36); those who have done evil will rise “unto the resurrection of damnation” (John 5:28-29); God gave his Son so that people “should not perish” (John 3:16). Paul: “the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom 2:5-8); those who do not obey the gospel “shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord” (2 Thess 1:9). Revelation, traditionally linked with John though its authorship is debated, uses the “lake of fire” (Rev 20:14-15).

So what does the silence mean? Christians read it in four main ways. (1) *Traditional view*: same reality, different vocabulary. Gehenna was a local Jerusalem image Jesus used with Jewish hearers; Paul wrote mainly to non-Jews and used words like wrath and destruction. (2) *Conditional immortality*: Paul and John speak of death, perishing and destruction, which suggests the end of the wicked rather than endless torment (Edward Fudge). (3) *Christian universalism*: Paul’s hope that “in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor 15:22) and that God will reconcile all things (Col 1:20) suggests judgement is purifying and not final (Thomas Talbott, David Bentley Hart). (4) *A union reading*, close to the learner’s: John and Paul frame everything as life in union with God versus death outside it, so the real question is relationship, not a place. Each view must account for all the texts above. The app’s afterlife pages set out each view in full.
50487:
The chain also runs in a good direction. If we begin with true presuppositions (God is exactly like Jesus, Heb 1:3; humans are made in his image and restored in Christ, Col 3:10), we will read the Bible as a story that leads to him. Our theology will see a Father who runs to the prodigal (Luke 15:20). Our eschatology will hope for new creation, not escape (Rom 8:19-21; Rev 21:5). Our ecclesiology will see the church as a family and a body, a foretaste of that new creation (Eph 2:19-22). And our lifestyle will bear the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22-23).

Two cautions keep this from becoming a slogan. First, the chain is a teaching picture, not a law: real life runs both ways. Our habits and worship also shape what we believe (an old Christian saying is *lex orandi, lex credendi*: the law of prayer is the law of belief), and the philosopher James K. A. Smith argues that our loves are formed by practices before ideas. Second, even right ideas do not save; Jesus does. The goal is not a perfect theory but a living union with the Person at the source of the river.
50488: The learner’s chain: how bad assumptions become a bad life
50489: Start at the root. Each link feeds the next. Example in each step: an angry, distant picture of God.

50499: The church becomes a holding room for the saved, a fortress against outsiders, or a machine for control.

50521: What would Jesus do? What should I do?

50525: Vicarious: lived for us and shared with us (Gal 2:20)

50535: Can produce earnest discipleship, but also pride or exhaustion
50536: Rest, confidence and love, with obedience as overflow

50540: Judgement language across the New Testament
50541: Gehenna is absent from John and Paul, but judgement is not.
50547: Fire, outer darkness, weeping; warnings to insiders
50550: Perishing, condemnation, wrath remaining, resurrection to judgement
50553: Wrath, death, destruction, exclusion from the Lord’s presence
50556: The tongue “set on fire of hell”
50558: The second death; Death and Hades thrown into the lake of fire
50560: The human is unknowable apart from the saving incarnation of Jesus Christ. For thousands of years, we watched ourselves bleed and guessed what a human might be. We offered sacrifices, built systems, and called our best efforts holiness. But the human remains a mystery until Jesus walks into time. He is not a superhuman; he is the human.
50561: Tragic ontology is the attempt to use Adam's perspective to interpret Christ's redemptive acts and sees Jesus' life as exemplary rather than vicarious. What to do, rather than Who you are…. Tragic ontology endeavors to make the flesh more holy by "copying" Jesus rather than recognizing its co-death in Christ and finding life and being in union with Jesus. The reality of redemption can't be understood by the reasoning inherited by Adam through the fall.
50562: He was made man that we might be made God.
50565: John Calvin (*Institutes* 3.1.1); Eastern Orthodox theosis; T. F. and J. B. Torrance (*Worship, Community and the Triune God of Grace*, 1996); Constantine Campbell (*Paul and Union with Christ*, 2012); Tommy Miller
50566: Salvation is participation in Christ: his death, resurrection and life become ours by the Spirit. Christian living is learning to live from what is already true. Jesus’ humanity is vicarious: he believes, obeys and worships on our behalf, and we share in it.
50567: Matches Paul’s pervasive “in Christ” language and John’s “abide”. Frees people from performance and shame. Unites justification and transformation in one Person.
50568: If taught carelessly it can sound as if obedience does not matter. Some worry it blurs the line between Creator and creature, which Orthodox and Reformed writers both work hard to guard.
50569: Following Jesus: the way of discipleship
50570: Thomas à Kempis (*The Imitation of Christ*, c. 1420s); the Anabaptist tradition of *Nachfolge* (following); Dietrich Bonhoeffer (*Discipleship*, 1937); Charles Sheldon (*In His Steps*, 1896)
50571: Jesus calls people to follow him, not merely to believe ideas about him. Grace that does not lead to obedience is what Bonhoeffer called “cheap grace”. Imitating Christ, including in suffering and love of enemies, is the shape of a real faith.
50572: Takes the Sermon on the Mount and Jesus’ call “follow me” seriously. Has produced martyrs, peacemakers and reformers.
50573: Can slide into moralism if separated from union and grace. Bonhoeffer himself grounded discipleship in Christ’s call and presence, not in self-effort, so the best of this view is not ‘imitation alone’.
50575: Mainstream Reformed and evangelical scholarship (Herman Ridderbos, *Paul: An Outline of His Theology*; Douglas Moo; Thomas Schreiner); also Catholic and Wesleyan writers on grace and cooperation
50576: Paul never sets identity against effort. He says “you have died” and then “put to death” (Col 3:3-5); “work out your own salvation… for it is God which worketh in you” (Phil 2:12-13). Union is the ground; real, Spirit-empowered effort is the response.
50577: Holds all the texts together. Guards against both moralism and passivity.
50578: Union-first writers answer that in practice the imperative often swallows the indicative in preaching, which is exactly the problem the learner is naming.
50579: The chain is real but runs both ways
50580: James K. A. Smith (*Desiring the Kingdom*, 2009); the ancient principle *lex orandi, lex credendi*
50581: Humans are not only thinkers but lovers and worshippers. Our practices and habits shape our beliefs as much as our beliefs shape our practices. So the chain needs a loop: change can start at the lifestyle end too, through worship, community and service.
50582: Fits how people actually change. Explains why sound doctrine sometimes coexists with bad living, and why a changed community can change minds.
50583: Can underplay the role of truth and teaching, which the New Testament stresses (1 Tim 4:16). Supporters of the chain reply that it describes the main direction, not the only one.
50584: “Since I am in Christ, effort and obedience no longer matter.”
50585: Some grace teaching is heard as saying that union with Christ makes commands, discipline and effort unnecessary, even legalistic.
50586: Paul’s union passages are always followed by commands. Romans 6 moves from “we are buried with him” (Rom 6:4) to “let not sin therefore reign” and “yield yourselves unto God” (Rom 6:12-13). Union is the power for obedience, not a replacement for it.
50587: Traditional evangelical and Reformed teachers (e.g. Sinclair Ferguson, *The Whole Christ*, 2016) agree that legalism and antinomianism (lawlessness) are twin errors with one cure: Christ himself. Union-first writers usually agree; they object to commands without identity, not to commands as such.
50588: The goal of the healthy chain is a changed life. A union that bears no fruit is not what John or Paul meant (John 15:5).
50589: “John and Paul never mention hell, so they did not believe in judgement.”
50590: The absence of the word Gehenna is taken to mean John and Paul taught no judgement at all.
50591: Both speak clearly of judgement in their own vocabulary: wrath remaining (John 3:36), resurrection to judgement (John 5:28-29), the day of wrath (Rom 2:5), everlasting destruction (2 Thess 1:9). The silence about Gehenna is real and worth asking about, but it is a silence about one image, not about judgement.
50592: Traditionalists argue the vocabulary changed with the audience, not the doctrine. Conditionalists and universalists argue the change of vocabulary matters for what judgement is like. All three agree the texts on judgement must be read, not ignored.
50593: Building a doctrine on what a text does not say is a form of the one-verse problem (Lesson 14). Honest reading weighs both the silence and the speech.

50609: Biblicist, Liberal, or the Heart of the Father?
50610: Is it enough to ask “Is it biblical?” What is the difference between a biblicist, a liberal, and someone who reads with the context and the heart of the Father?
50611: “Is it biblical?” is a good question that can give bad answers, because almost anything (polygamy, slavery, holy war) can be shown to be ‘in the Bible’. A better question is “Is it Christ-like, read in its context?” Biblicists, liberals and Christ-centred readers all love truth; they differ on where final authority lies and how the Bible’s hard parts are handled.
50613:
Christians often settle questions by asking, “Is it biblical?” The instinct is good: the Bereans checked even Paul against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). But the question has a weakness. Many things are “in the Bible” that no Christian today would practise. Abraham, Jacob and David had several wives, and the Law regulated polygamy rather than forbidding it (Exod 21:10; Deut 21:15). The Law permitted Israelites to own foreign slaves for life (Lev 25:44-46), and Paul told slaves to obey their masters (Eph 6:5). Israel was told to destroy whole peoples (Deut 7:2; 1 Sam 15:3).

If the Bible is treated as a rule book where every verse is an equal command for all times, these texts become weapons. The learner’s point is that the question must change: not only “Is it in the Bible?” but “Is it Christological?” In other words, does this reading fit what God has revealed in Jesus, the one in whom “the fulness of the Godhead” dwells bodily (Col 2:9)?

This lesson sets out three ways of answering, as fairly as possible: biblicism, liberal or progressive reading, and the Christ-centred contextual reading the learner holds. Many Christians blend elements of all three.
50615:
The word “biblicism” is used in two ways. The historian David Bebbington used it for one of the four marks of evangelicals: a deep love and high regard for the Bible (with conversion, the cross and active mission). In that broad sense most evangelicals happily call themselves biblicists.

The sociologist Christian Smith, in *The Bible Made Impossible* (2011), used the word more narrowly for a set of assumptions: that the Bible is clear to any sincere reader, that it addresses every subject of life, that its teaching is universally applicable, that it can be read by “common sense” without tradition, and that it works like a handbook for faith and practice. Smith’s argument is that this approach defeats itself, because the same Bible, read this way, produces endless disagreement (“pervasive interpretive pluralism”). His own answer is to read the Bible Christocentrically, as a witness to Christ.

The strengths of biblicism are real. It honours God’s words, gives ordinary believers access to Scripture, and resists fashion. It also deserves a fair hearing: careful inerrantist scholars such as D. A. Carson or Paul Copan are not naive literalists. They use genre, context, covenant and progressive revelation (Lesson 16) to explain why polygamy and holy war are not commands for today. Critics of Smith, including reviewers at The Gospel Coalition and Peter Leithart, argue that his critique hits popular biblicism but not the best evangelical scholarship.
50616: Liberal and progressive reading, fairly described
50617:
Liberal theology began with thinkers such as Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834), who wanted to keep faith credible after the Enlightenment. He located religion in the human experience of utter dependence on God. Adolf von Harnack (*What Is Christianity?*, 1900) sought the simple gospel of Jesus beneath later doctrine. In recent decades writers such as Marcus Borg (*Reading the Bible Again for the First Time*, 2001) read the Bible as a human witness to people’s experience of God, “historical and metaphorical”, and many progressive Christians today read it the same way.

The liberal instinct deserves respect. It takes science and history seriously, refuses to defend cruelty because a verse seems to command it, and has often been on the side of the poor and excluded. It is honest that the Bible contains human voices, including mistaken ones.

Its critics, from J. Gresham Machen (*Christianity and Liberalism*, 1923) to many today, argue that it makes the modern reader’s conscience the final judge of Scripture. If we decide in advance what God may be like, Jesus himself can be edited to fit, including his miracles and resurrection. Note that “progressive Christianity” is not the same thing as “progressive revelation” (Lesson 16): the first often relativises Scripture; the second says God revealed himself step by step, climaxing in Christ.
